opus-5.5.text:
I think they're two halves of the same process. A benchmark is ultimately a hypothesis about what intelligence is, or at least about some aspect of it you care about measuring. When you design a benchmark in isolation, you're making guesses about what will be hard, what will require genuine generalization, and what can be shortcut. Very often those guesses turn out to be wrong in ways you can't anticipate from the armchair.

The only way to find out is to actually try to solve it. When you attempt solutions, you discover the loopholes: the tasks that can be cracked by brute-force search, by memorizing patterns from the training distribution, or by exploiting some regularity in how the tasks were generated rather than through real abstraction. Every one of those discoveries tells you something about how to make the benchmark better. And the reverse is true too: watching where solution attempts fail tells you where the real difficulty lies, which sharpens your understanding of what you're measuring.

That's been very much my experience with ARC. Designing the tasks and thinking about how a system would approach them, whether that's program synthesis, deep learning, or some hybrid, were always intertwined. The benchmark shapes the research, and the research reveals the weaknesses of the benchmark. So you iterate. ARC-AGI-2 exists because we learned a lot from how people tackled the first version, including which tasks turned out to be susceptible to approaches that don't reflect fluid intelligence.

There's a deeper point too. If your benchmark designers never engage with solutions, you tend to end up with benchmarks that saturate quickly, because you've inadvertently measured something that can be bought with more data and more compute, rather than the ability to adapt to novelty. Good benchmark design means adversarially probing your own benchmark, and the best way to do that is to be a serious solver yourself. You want a benchmark that stays easy for humans and hard for AI for the right reasons, and you only learn what the right reasons are by trying to close that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says benchmark design and research should inform each other, but does not identify directing research toward bottlenecks to strong AI generalization as the purpose of creating ARC-1.

r002.rationale: It describes iterating from ARC to ARC-AGI-2, but does not assert that AI evaluation will continually require new benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says a good benchmark should stay easy for humans and hard for AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the two are really the same activity, looked at from different angles. A benchmark is a hypothesis. When you create one, you're saying: here is what I believe intelligence looks like, here is the capability I think is missing from current systems, and here is a way to measure it. But a hypothesis that nobody tries to falsify is not worth much. The only way to find out whether your benchmark actually captures what you think it captures is to try to solve it, and to watch other people try to solve it.

That's what happened with ARC. I put it out in 2019 with a fairly specific claim: that these tasks require on-the-fly program synthesis, the ability to take a few examples and build a new model of the situation, and that memorization at scale would not get you there. For a long time that held up. But what really taught me something was seeing the approaches that did start to work, things like test-time training, test-time search over programs, combining deep learning with discrete search. Those solutions told me which parts of the benchmark were measuring what I intended and which parts were exploitable by shortcuts I hadn't anticipated. You simply cannot learn that by sitting on the sidelines and only grading other people's submissions.

And there's the other direction too. If you're only building solutions, you tend to optimize for whatever metric is in front of you, and you lose sight of whether that metric still means anything. Benchmarks saturate. The moment a benchmark becomes a target, it starts to decouple from the underlying capability. So the person who is actually trying to solve the problem is in the best position to notice when the benchmark has stopped being informative, and to design the next one. ARC-AGI-2, and now what we're doing with ARC-AGI-3, came directly out of understanding, from the inside, where the first version was weak.

So I see it as a loop. You formalize an idea about intelligence as a benchmark. You attack it. The attack reveals the gap between what you wanted to measure and what you actually measured. You close that gap with a better benchmark. If you separate the two, if the benchmark designers and the solvers never talk to each other, both sides end up fooling themselves. The benchmark people think they've defined intelligence, and the solvers think they've achieved it, and neither is true.

r001.rationale: The response says ARC tasks require on-the-fly program synthesis and resist memorization, but does not identify directing research toward bottlenecks in strong AI generalization as ARC-1’s purpose.

r002.rationale: It says benchmarks saturate and describes creating better, successive benchmarks as part of an ongoing cycle, supporting the need for new benchmarks over time.

r003.rationale: It describes ARC tasks as requiring new models from a few examples, but does not propose choosing tasks that are hard for AI and easy for humans.

astra-6.text:
Because a benchmark is really an expression of what you think the problem is. You’re saying, “This is the capability we care about, and this is how we’re going to measure it.” But until you try to build a system that has that capability, you don’t really know whether your formulation is right. You may be measuring something else. There may be shortcuts that let you do well on the benchmark without solving the underlying problem.

So there needs to be a feedback loop. You formulate the problem, you try to solve it, and what you learn from trying to solve it helps you refine the formulation. Likewise, having an explicit benchmark forces you to make your ideas concrete. You can’t just say that your system is more general or better at reasoning—you have to explain what that means operationally.

Of course, you don’t want to design a benchmark just to make your own approach look good. The goal is to develop the measurement and the understanding of the problem together, while keeping the evaluation independent enough that it can tell you when you’re wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes refining a benchmark and its solution together, but does not identify directing research toward bottlenecks to strong AI generalization as ARC-1’s purpose.

r002.rationale: It argues for a feedback loop between benchmarks and solutions, but does not assert that AI evaluation will continually require new benchmarks.

r003.rationale: It does not propose selecting tasks that are difficult for AI but easy for humans.

sol-6.1.text:
Because developing a solution is how you find out what your benchmark actually measures. You may design a task that you think requires abstraction or reasoning, but then discover that a relatively simple shortcut gets a high score. That tells you something about the task, and you need to incorporate that feedback into the benchmark.

At the same time, you need a clear idea of what capability you’re trying to measure, independently of the systems you happen to be building. Otherwise, you can end up designing a benchmark that flatters your own approach. So there should be a feedback loop: you formulate a definition of the capability, you build a test, you try to solve it, and you use what you learn to improve both your understanding and the test. A benchmark is a scientific instrument. Developing it involves checking that it measures what you think it measures.
